# flai command reference

Every command, subcommand, and flag, as `flai --help` prints them. The guide, with how the commands fit together, is [flai.md](flai.md).

| Command | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| [accept](#flai-accept) | Accept an item: merge its branch, move to done, archive, commit |
| [adr](#flai-adr) | Record architecture decisions |

| [analyze](#flai-analyze) | Start the analyzer for the project: it looks for bottlenecks, intent, or risk and writes one report under design/analysis |

## flai

Manage monorepos that follow the system-flow standard.

flai creates and imports projects that follow the system-flow standard, manages work items and agent narratives, validates the repository, prints flow metrics, and runs the flaiover dashboard.

Configuration is read from ~/.flai/config.json (override with --config or FLAI\_CONFIG). Every command that prints data accepts --json.

Global flags, accepted by every command:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--config` string | path to config file (default ~/.flai/config.json, or $FLAI\_CONFIG) |
| `--json` | print structured JSON output |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | debug-level log events on stderr (LOG\_LEVEL, LOG\_FORMAT also apply) |
| `-y`, `--yes` | answer yes to confirmations |

### flai accept

Accept an item: merge its branch, move to done, archive, commit.

```text
flai accept <id> [flags]
```

The operator's acceptance step as one command, per design/conventions/work-management.md and git.md:

```text
0. rebase the story branch and fast-forward it into the main branch
1. move the item to done (its rules apply: children closed, criteria checked);
   a story's epic follows it, to done when it was the epic's last open story
2. flai archive for the item and its children and narrative, and for an
   epic that followed its story to done, the epic and its cancelled stories;
   every thread still open or answered on what is archived is resolved,
   as "<id> was accepted", by whoever accepts (I-0073), and every
   conversation still open of a story archived is closed, as "<id> was
   accepted", or "<id> was archived" for an epic's cancelled story (ADR-0120)
3. git commit the work item, the archive, the threads, and the
   conversations; while another git process holds the index lock, git add
   and git commit are run again, for about nine seconds in all, and the
   lock is never removed
4. tell every story in progress or in review whose touches cover a path
   the merge changed which paths those are, for its agent's MCP inbox
```

Under acceptance.mode: pull-request (ADR-0170), step 0 merges no branch on this machine. Once the pull request's checks and reviews pass (ADR-0169), it refuses, naming them, while the main branch has commits not on origin's main that change paths outside the wip folder; merges the story's pull request on the forge by acceptance.merge\_method, at the head the checks passed at, and deletes the story's branch on origin; fetches main and brings the main branch up to origin's, rebasing its unpublished wip commits onto it in a temporary worktree and moving it with git reset --keep, which keeps uncommitted edits; and removes the story's worktree and branch. The merge is made here when the forge's token can be read here, while the forge host action is on; otherwise flai serve on the host makes it, and flai accept waits for its answer (the dashboard's acceptance never hands it over). A pull request merged on the forge already is accepted with no second merge, and a merge the forge refuses stops the acceptance, with its reason, before anything changes here. Steps 1 to 4 are as under local acceptance.

Acceptance computes no release, creates no tag, and pushes nothing (S-0087): that is a deliberate step of its own, run when the operator chooses to publish what has accumulated on main, not tied to any one item. See flai release --pending.

flai move &lt;story&gt; done from review runs exactly this. An item that is already done but was never archived (an older flai, a hand edit) is completed from step 0 without a second transition. An item that is done and archived while its archived file is not committed is one whose commit failed: the error kept git's output and named this command. It is completed by resolving the threads and closing the conversations left open on what it archived, as step 2 does, and from step 3, committing what the main checkout holds under the usual subject, and step 4 tells the open stories the paths the story's commits changed. A done, archived item whose file is committed is refused as already done. The orchestrator completes either only when it made the move to done itself; one anyone else made is the operator's to complete, and the refusal names who made it (ADR-0189). --dry-run changes nothing.

A story whose branch changes a path Claude Code protects (a .claude folder, .mcp.json, and the others of ADR-0106) is accepted by its operator only: the story's owner or the project's owner, or anyone but the orchestrator when neither is named. Anyone else is refused, before anything is merged, with the files named; --dry-run lists them.

Markdown flai accept commits passes the project's lint (S-0367): the fix command of each test tier that has one runs over what the main checkout has not committed before anything changes and again before step 3's commit, and step 0's rebase runs it over what the story branch changes. When a tier's check still fails on those files, the acceptance is refused with each file, line, and error, before anything changes or before the merge; correct them and accept again. --dry-run runs neither. With --json that refusal exits 4 and prints {"refused": {"id", "reason", "findings"}}, each finding with its tier, checkout (main, or story with the story's ID), path, line, column, level, rule, alias, and message, as markdownlint-cli2 gives them (S-0378).

--by orchestrator is the orchestrator's acceptance (ADR-0093), refused unless orchestration.permissions.accept\_reviews is on; under FLAI\_ROLE=orchestrate no other acceptance is allowed. It is refused, before anything is merged, unless --verified names the story branch's head, every acceptance criterion is ticked, every file the branch changes is under the story's touches and on no path Claude Code protects, no thread on the story or its tasks is open, and --evidence, a Verdict: line and one item "- &lt;n&gt;: &lt;files&gt;" per criterion, names a changed file for each of them. It leaves the main checkout's uncommitted files outside wip as the merge queue's landing does, --yes or not: out of the lint fix and the acceptance commit. It is refused only while the story's change, main...story/&lt;id&gt;, would overwrite one of them or an untracked one; --dry-run lists that as the blocker dirty\_main, naming the files and the command that sets them aside (ADR-0189). When its rebase of the story branch stops on conflicts that the merge of the issue files, the ADR index, the issue summary, and the shared markdown files does not settle, it aborts the rebase, moves the story back to in-progress as flai with the paths in the reason, opens one thread on the story naming them and the branch, which flai serve starts the story's agent on, and exits saying the story was sent back; with --json it exits 4 and prints {"refused": {"id", "reason", "sent\_back", "branch", "base", "conflicts", "thread"}}. Any other acceptance leaves the stopped rebase in the worktree (ADR-0189). The evidence is written, with the commit, under ### Accepted by the orchestrator in the story's Notes. With --dry-run the evidence is optional. While the merge-queue host action is on and the queue batches (accept\_reviews on, under local acceptance), --by orchestrator is refused, naming the queue, but as the queue's landing or with --dry-run: the orchestrator enqueues the story instead, with flai queue add &lt;id&gt; --by orchestrator --verified &lt;commit&gt; --evidence &lt;file&gt; or the MCP tool queue\_add, and the queue lands it (S-0403).

A story whose rebased branch undoes the main branch's change to a path, as a revert replayed over main's identical change does (ADR-0155, I-0124), is refused before anything is merged while the path is not kept: each path flai stream sync recorded and its branch still undoes, and each path the acceptance's own rebase finds. --dry-run lists each under undoes\_main, with main's lines the branch removes, and each not kept as a blocker. Restore main's version with flai stream restore &lt;id&gt; --path &lt;path&gt;, send the story back to in-progress, or, as the operator, keep the removal with --keep-removal &lt;path&gt; (repeatable) and --reason "&lt;why&gt;": one --reason per --keep-removal in order, or one for them all. A --keep-removal naming a path the record does not hold, one without a reason, a reason on more than one line, and any with --by orchestrator are refused before anything changes: an undone path waits for the operator. Each kept path and its reason are written, with the commit, under ### Removals kept in the story's Notes. With --json the refusal exits 4 and prints {"refused": {"id", "reason", "undoes\_main"}}, each path with its path, lines, and old\_base.

--batch &lt;id&gt; is the merge queue's landing (ADR-0176): flai serve runs it for each story of a batch that passed, in queue order, as whoever enqueued the story. It takes the batch's verification in place of the story head's own: the verified commit is the story's rebased head in the batch. It is refused, before anything is merged, unless the queue's batch is the one named, is not dropped, and lets the story land, the story is the next of it to land, the story's branch is still at the head the batch rebased a copy of, and the main branch is where the batch's landing left it. With --by orchestrator it needs no --verified, which it is refused beside, and no --evidence; the batch and its verified commit are written under ### Accepted by the orchestrator, with the evidence when given, else the evidence the orchestrator enqueued the story with and, as Enqueued verified, the commit its verifier checked then; a story enqueued without them lands with the batch's verification alone. The story is recorded as landed in the queue's state, and the batch kept, where an acceptance without --batch takes the story out of the queue and drops the batch that holds it. Under acceptance.mode: pull-request, which has no merge queue, it is refused, and under FLAI\_ROLE=orchestrate too: the orchestrator never lands a story by hand.

Examples:

```bash
flai accept S-031 --by alex
flai accept S-031 --by alex --dry-run
flai accept S-031 --by orchestrator --verified 4f1c2a9 --dry-run
flai accept S-031 --by orchestrator --verified 4f1c2a9 --evidence evidence.md
flai accept S-031 --by alex --keep-removal docs/guide.md --reason "the story rewrites the section"
flai accept S-031 --by orchestrator --batch 20261019-041200
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--batch` string | the merge queue batch whose verification the acceptance takes, as flai serve lands it (ADR-0176) |
| `--by` string | who accepted (default: config author) |
| `--dry-run` | show what would block acceptance and change nothing |
| `--evidence` string | with --by orchestrator: file holding its evidence, a Verdict: line and - &lt;n&gt;: &lt;files&gt; per criterion (- reads standard input) |
| `--keep-removal` stringArray | as the operator: accept the branch's removal of the main branch's lines at this recorded path, with --reason (repeatable) |
| `--reason` stringArray | with --keep-removal: why the removal is kept, one per --keep-removal in order or one for all (repeatable) |
| `--trailer` stringArray | line appended to the commit message (repeatable) |
| `--verified` string | with --by orchestrator: the commit its verifier passed, the story branch's head |

### flai adr

Record architecture decisions.

Subcommands:

- [accept](#flai-adr-accept): Accept a proposed ADR: status accepted, dated today, index row updated
- [new](#flai-adr-new): Record a new ADR: number, file, front matter, and index row are supplied
- [topics](#flai-adr-topics): Set the topics of an ADR of any status, and nothing else

#### flai adr accept

Accept a proposed ADR: status accepted, dated today, index row updated.

```text
flai adr accept <number> [flags]
```

Only a proposed ADR can be accepted. Once accepted an ADR is immutable except for superseded\_by and topics: to change the decision, record a new ADR that supersedes it.

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--autocommit` | commit the change on its own, unless dashboard.autocommit is false |
| `--trailer` stringArray | trailer line for the commit (repeatable) |

#### flai adr new

Record a new ADR: number, file, front matter, and index row are supplied.

```text
flai adr new "<title>" [flags]
```

Record an architecture decision. The number is one more than the highest NNNN-\*.md in design/adrs in this checkout, on main, in any story's worktree (uncommitted files included), and on any story branch, so parallel stories do not take the same number; gaps are not filled. The file is NNNN-slug.md with id, title, status, date, supersedes, superseded\_by, and refines when given; its row is added to design/adrs/README.md; each ADR it supersedes gets superseded\_by set, the one edit allowed to an accepted ADR.

The body below the heading is the project's 0000-template.md sections, or standard input with --body-stdin. flai check runs with everything in place: if it reports anything the ADR introduces, every file is put back, the findings are printed, and the exit code is 4. --autocommit commits the new file, the index, and any superseded ADRs on their own, unless the project sets dashboard.autocommit: false. Nothing is pushed. --print-body prints the template's sections and creates nothing.

--commit, run in a story's worktree, instead commits what was written, the new file, the index, and any superseded ADRs, and nothing else, on the story's branch as "docs: [S-nnnn] ADR-nnnn &lt;title&gt;", with each --trailer, and adds them to the story's touches in the main checkout. The story is FLAI\_STORY, else the one in FLAI\_AGENT of the form agent-S-nnnn, else the story branch checked out. The output then says what was committed and what the touches gained; --json adds commit (null when nothing changed), which takes the place of --autocommit's, and touches\_added. Where the story's branch is not checked out, or no story resolves, --commit is refused and nothing is written; so is --commit with --autocommit.

Examples:

```bash
flai adr new "Dashboards authenticate with a project token" --status accepted --refines 16
flai adr new "Replace the SPA with server rendering" --supersedes 7 --body-stdin --autocommit < decision.md
flai adr new "Issues are committed on the story's branch" --body-stdin --commit --json < decision.md
flai adr new --print-body
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--autocommit` | commit what was written on its own, unless dashboard.autocommit is false |
| `--body-stdin` | read the body below the heading from standard input |
| `--commit` | commit what was written on the story's branch, checked out here in its worktree, as docs: [S-nnnn] ..., and add it to the story's touches; refused, with nothing written, where no story's branch is checked out |
| `--print-body` | print the template's sections and create nothing |
| `--refines` strings | ADR this one refines (repeatable) |
| `--status` string | proposed or accepted (default `proposed`) |
| `--supersedes` strings | ADR this one supersedes (repeatable): 7, 0007, or ADR-0007 |
| `--trailer` stringArray | trailer line for the commit, --autocommit's or --commit's (repeatable) |

#### flai adr topics

Set the topics of an ADR of any status, and nothing else.

```text
flai adr topics <number> <topic>... [flags]
```

Set which stories an ADR is for (ADR-0047): topics replaces the topics key in the ADR's front matter, or adds it at the end, and changes nothing else. With superseded\_by it is the one key an accepted ADR may gain. A topic is a word; all is every story, and the others are the words flai check knows: each sub-project's name, tags, and kind in system-flow.yaml, and code. Topics may be separate arguments or comma separated. flai check runs with the change in place: a finding it introduces, such as a topic nothing uses, puts the file back and exits 4.

Examples:

```bash
flai adr topics ADR-0019 cli template
flai adr topics 47 all --autocommit
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--autocommit` | commit the change on its own, unless dashboard.autocommit is false |
| `--trailer` stringArray | trailer line for the commit (repeatable) |

### flai agent

The project's default agent: the harness, model, and options every new story gets.

```text
flai agent
```

Who works a story is an agent: a harness (the command line or API that runs it, such as claude-code), a model (such as claude-opus-5-5), and options for that harness (config, key=value). It may name a provider, the endpoint the model's calls go to, by a name the host sets with flai serve agent provider &lt;name&gt; (ADR-0129); with none, the harness's own. The project's default is kept in system-flow.yaml; every story created while it is set gets a copy in its front matter, which flai story new --harness/--model/--provider/--agent-config and flai edit override for that story. Stories created before, or with no default set, carry none.

An agent may also name roles: the agents for the work a story's agent hands to sub-agents, explore and verify (S-0189), each with a harness, model, and config of its own (--role-harness, --role-model, --role-config). flai serve starts claude-code with each role's model over the project's sub-agent definition for it.

flai agent shows the default, set changes it (only what you give; --config adds or replaces keys, --role-config role.key= removes one, --unset-role removes a role), and clear removes it.

Examples:

```bash
flai agent
flai agent set --harness claude-code --model claude-opus-5-5 --config effort=high
flai agent set --model claude-sonnet-5
flai agent set --provider litellm
flai agent set --role-model explore=haiku --role-model verify=sonnet
flai agent clear
```

Subcommands:

- [clear](#flai-agent-clear): Remove the project's default agent; stories keep what they have
- [set](#flai-agent-set): Set the project's default harness, model, or options

#### flai agent clear

Remove the project's default agent; stories keep what they have.

```text
flai agent clear [flags]
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--autocommit` | commit system-flow.yaml on its own, unless dashboard.autocommit is false |
| `--trailer` stringArray | a trailer line for the commit (repeatable) |

#### flai agent set

Set the project's default harness, model, or options.

```text
flai agent set [flags]
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--autocommit` | commit system-flow.yaml on its own, unless dashboard.autocommit is false |
| `--config` stringArray | an option for the harness, key=value (repeatable) |
| `--harness` string | the harness that runs the agent, such as claude-code |
| `--model` string | the model it runs, such as claude-opus-5-5 |
| `--provider` string | the provider the model's calls go to, a name the host sets with flai serve agent provider &lt;name&gt;, such as litellm |
| `--replace` | start from nothing: the default becomes exactly what is given |
| `--role-config` stringArray | an option for a sub-agent role, role.key=value (repeatable) |
| `--role-harness` stringArray | the harness of a sub-agent role, role=harness, such as verify=claude-code (repeatable) |
| `--role-model` stringArray | the model a sub-agent role runs, role=model, such as verify=sonnet (repeatable) |
| `--trailer` stringArray | a trailer line for the commit (repeatable) |
| `--unset` stringArray | remove an option by key (repeatable) |
| `--unset-role` stringArray | remove a sub-agent role (repeatable) |

### flai analyze

Start the analyzer for the project: it looks for bottlenecks, intent, or risk and writes one report under design/analysis.

```text
flai analyze [flags]
```

Starts the analyzer for the project, now, on this host and as you (S-0223). It runs in the project's main checkout with the project's analysis agent: analysis.agent in system-flow.yaml over the project's agent, started with the harnesses and the command you set with flai serve agent. It reads the metrics, the design, the code, and the issues, looks for what --focus names, or for all of it without one: bottlenecks in the flow, gaps between design/system and the code (intent), and technical and security risks (risk). It writes one report under design/analysis, edits nothing else, and authors no stories.

The run is recorded where flai serve tracks agents, as the analyzer's, the newest alone, and its output goes to a log beside flai serve's state. Once it ends, the serving flai records how (worked or failed) and logs the report it wrote and what the run cost in wip/agents/analyzer.md. It is no story's agent: the in-progress limit does not count it, and it holds no story back. One analyzer runs for a project at a time.

It is a host action, off until you enable it (flai serve enable analyze). It refuses, and says why, while the action is off for the project, for a focus other than bottlenecks, intent, or risk, while an analyzer runs for the project, naming it, and when nothing can start it. The host API's analyze.run runs this, and analysis.schedule in system-flow.yaml starts it on a schedule while flai serve runs.

Examples:

```bash
flai serve enable analyze
flai analyze
flai analyze --focus risk --json
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--focus` string | what to look for: bottlenecks, intent, or risk; all three when not given |

### flai archive

Move done and cancelled items and their narratives to wip/archive.

```text
flai archive [id...] [flags]
```

Without IDs, every closed epic, every closed story with its tasks, and every closed task whose story is no longer on the board is archived. With IDs, each must be done or cancelled; a story brings its tasks and narrative.

Every thread still open or answered on an item archived is resolved, as "&lt;id&gt; was archived", so that none is left open on an archived item (I-0073), and every conversation still open of a story archived is closed, with the entry "Closed: &lt;id&gt; was archived" (ADR-0120). Nothing is committed. --dry-run names the threads it would resolve and the conversations it would close.

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--dry-run` | print the plan without moving anything |

### flai block

Open a blocked interval on an item.

```text
flai block <id> [flags]
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--reason` string | why the item is blocked |

### flai board

Print the kanban board.

```text
flai board [flags]
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--all` | include epics and tasks |

Subcommands:

- [limit](#flai-board-limit): Set a column's WIP limit

#### flai board limit

Set a column's WIP limit.

```text
flai board limit <column> <n>
```

Set the WIP limit of ready, in-progress, or review in wip/kanban/board.md, the one place flai, flai serve, flai check, and the dashboard read it from. 0 removes the limit. Limits count stories; a move past one warns.

Examples:

```bash
flai board limit in-progress 3
flai board limit review 0
```

### flai check

Validate the repository against the system-flow standard.

```text
flai check [dir] [flags]
```

Check the manifest, layout, every work item in kanban and archive, the narratives and their index, the board, and documentation front matter.

Findings print as path:line: level: rule: message. Errors exit 1; with --strict warnings do too, except two that only the operator clears: the review column over its limit, which acceptance clears, and an epic behind its stories (epic.lags-stories), which moving or accepting the epic clears.

With --story S-nnnn, a finding is inside the story when it is on the story's item file or one of its tasks', its narrative, a thread anchored on the story or one of its tasks, or a path its branch changes against the main branch (as flai stream diff reads it), or that is uncommitted in its worktree. Every other finding is outside it. A wip.overlap that names the story is outside it too, and one between two other stories is left out, as is an item.archive outside the story, which only flai archive in the main checkout clears, a board.wip-limit outside the story, which counts the main checkout's columns and only the operator's acceptances, cancellations, or a raised limit clear, an issues.no-story outside the story, which names an issue the story did not touch and only the operator's choice to make a story for it clears, a threads.archived outside the story, an open or answered thread on an archived item that only the operator or the thread's opener resolves in the main checkout, the note components.examples gives when it could not check examples for want of node or a sub-project's svelte, unless the story changes a file under the folder it names, which only installing the tool clears, and a markdown or narrative.state finding on the narrative of another story that is neither done nor cancelled, which that story's own close-out finds. A finding outside keeps its level and is printed with "(outside S-nnnn)"; it is a note that neither an error nor --strict fails on, and the summary counts it, as does outside in --json. Without --story every finding counts, as the main branch's check needs.

--story takes several stories, comma-separated or repeated, as a merge queue batch names the stories it verifies: a finding is inside when it is inside any of them, and outside only when it is outside every one, printed with "(outside S-0001, S-0002)". A wip.overlap is outside when it names any of them and left out when it names none, and a markdown or narrative.state finding is left out on the narrative of an open story that is none of them.

With --record-issues and one story, each rule with findings outside the story is recorded in design/issues, in the checkout the run reads, which is the story's worktree at close-out. A wip.overlap is not recorded: the pull hold and the other story's agent clear it. Each rule is recorded in the open issue whose title names it, as "flai check finds `story.unaccepted` outside the story at close-out" does, opened with class efficiency when none is, with an instance naming the story and each finding's path and message. An instance for the same story and the same findings is written once, so running the check again does not count it again; another story, or other findings, bump the count. summary.md is regenerated, each issue is printed as opened, bumped, or already recorded, and --json lists them in recorded. The run records whether or not it passes; a failure to record is an error. With several stories --record-issues is refused: it records a close-out's findings, and a batch records none.

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--record-issues` | with --story and one story, record each rule's findings outside the story in an issue, opening or bumping it once per story and findings |
| `--story` strings | scope the run to a story (S-nnnn), or to several, comma-separated or repeated: findings outside every one are notes that do not fail it |
| `--strict` | treat warnings as failures, except the review column over its limit and an epic behind its stories |

### flai checks

Run, watch, and cancel checks for a story in review.

Subcommands:

- [cancel](#flai-checks-cancel): Stop an active run: terminate, then, if it has not gone, kill
- [run](#flai-checks-run): Run every named check, in order, in the story's worktree; refuses a second run while one is active
- [status](#flai-checks-status): The current or last run for a story: which check, pass or fail so far, outcome and duration once ended
- [tail](#flai-checks-tail): New output since --from, waiting for more while the run is active

#### flai checks cancel

Stop an active run: terminate, then, if it has not gone, kill.

```text
flai checks cancel <story-id> [flags]
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--grace-seconds` int | how long to wait for the run to stop before giving up on reporting it (the kill itself has its own, shorter grace period) (default `10`) |

#### flai checks run

Run every named check, in order, in the story's worktree; refuses a second run while one is active.

```text
flai checks run <story-id>
```

Runs each check named in flai serve checks set, or, when it names none, the manifest's checks:, in order, in the story's worktree, stopping at the first to fail. Bounded by the configured time limit (flai serve checks timeout); flai checks cancel stops it early. This blocks until the run ends, real minutes, not seconds; the outcome and duration stay with the story (flai checks status) until it is accepted.

#### flai checks status

The current or last run for a story: which check, pass or fail so far, outcome and duration once ended.

```text
flai checks status <story-id>
```

#### flai checks tail

New output since --from, waiting for more while the run is active.

```text
flai checks tail <story-id> [flags]
```

Reads the run's log from --from, an offset in bytes into the file (0 for the start), and prints each new complete line as it is found. While the run is still active it polls for up to --wait seconds for more before returning; the answer's offset is where to --from next time. Meant to be called in a loop for as long as the review page (or a shell) wants to keep watching.

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--from` int | byte offset into the log to read from |
| `--wait` int | seconds to wait for more output while the run is active (default `20`) |

### flai cod

Print an epic's or story's cost of delay per week, from its inputs or its epic's share.

```text
flai cod <E-nnnn|S-nnnn>
```

Works out what each week of waiting for an epic or a story costs, in planning.currency. From the item's own cost of delay inputs, the value per week is revenue\_per\_week plus penalty\_per\_week plus the hours of time\_lost\_per\_cycle times planning.hour\_rate times the cycles in a week (a week over planning.cycle, 168h by default); time lost needs planning.hour\_rate. A story without inputs of its own takes a share of its epic's value, worked out from the epic's inputs or, without them, the value recorded on it: the share its forecast duration is of the durations of the epic's open stories without inputs, each its own forecast.duration or one worked out from history as flai forecast does. An epic without inputs, or a story with neither inputs nor an epic that has inputs or a value, is refused: the inputs are the operator's to give, with flai edit --revenue-per-week, --penalty-per-week, and --time-lost-per-cycle. Amounts are rounded to two decimals. flai cod writes nothing; record the result with flai edit --cost-of-delay-value.

Examples:

```bash
flai cod E-0016
flai cod S-0210 --json
```

### flai components

List the component library: each Svelte sub-project's components and their props.

The component library is the components of the project's Svelte sub-projects, those whose kind in system-flow.yaml is sveltekit or svelte (ADR-0162). A sub-project's components are its .svelte files that match its components.include globs, src/lib/\*\*/\*.svelte by default, and none of its components.exclude globs; its components.setup names a module the harness imports before any component, such as the app's stylesheet.

flai components list prints the catalogue, each component with the props it takes, read by the sub-project's own svelte/compiler; flai components config writes a sub-project's components key, which flai manifest set does not reach; flai components serve runs a sub-project's own Vite dev server with flai's harness, which renders one component by its path (ADR-0163).

Examples:

```bash
flai components list
flai components list --project flaiover --json
flai components config flaiover --setup src/routes/layout.css
flai components serve --project flaiover
flai components serve --project flaiover --story S-0042
```

Subcommands:

- [config](#flai-components-config): Write a Svelte sub-project's components key: its include and exclude globs and its setup
- [list](#flai-components-list): Print each Svelte sub-project's components and the props each takes
- [serve](#flai-components-serve): Run a Svelte sub-project's own Vite dev server with flai's component harness, in the foreground

#### flai components config

Write a Svelte sub-project's components key: its include and exclude globs and its setup.

```text
flai components config <sub-project> [flags]
```

Write the components key of the sub-project the argument names in system-flow.yaml, keeping every other key, the order, and the comments.

Each flag given replaces its field of the key as it is; a field whose flag is not given keeps its value, so --setup alone keeps the globs. --include and --exclude are repeatable, and the globs given replace the field's whole list. A glob is relative to the sub-project's folder, with segments separated by /, each a path.Match pattern or \*\* alone, which stands for any number of folders. --setup is a module of the sub-project, relative to its folder, that the harness imports before any component; --setup "" removes it. --unset removes the key, so that the defaults apply: include src/lib/\*\*/\*.svelte, nothing excluded, no setup. It is given alone.

The manifest is checked as it would be after the change, as flai check checks it. A sub-project whose kind is not sveltekit or svelte, a glob that does not parse, or a setup that names no file under the sub-project's folder is refused with the field and the reason, and nothing is written; the exit status is 1, as for a workflow rule's refusal. With --json a refusal is {"refused": [{"field": ..., "reason": ...}]} on standard output, and a change {"project": ..., "components": {"include": [...], "exclude": [...], "setup": ...}}, components null after --unset.

Examples:

```bash
flai components config flaiover --setup src/routes/layout.css
flai components config ui --include 'src/lib/**/*.svelte' --include 'src/widgets/*.svelte'
flai components config ui --exclude 'src/lib/internal/**' --json
flai components config ui --unset
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--exclude` stringArray | a glob of files include finds that are not components (repeatable; replaces the list) |
| `--include` stringArray | a glob of the sub-project's component files, relative to its folder (repeatable; replaces the list) |
| `--setup` string | a module of the sub-project the harness imports before any component, such as src/app.css; "" removes it |
| `--unset` | remove the components key, so that the defaults apply |

#### flai components list

Print each Svelte sub-project's components and the props each takes.

```text
flai components list [flags]
```

Print the component library: every sub-project of system-flow.yaml, in its order, or only the one --project names. A sub-project of kind sveltekit or svelte is listed with its components, each a .svelte file its components key finds, by its path relative to the sub-project, and under it each prop: its name, its kind (string, number, boolean, union with its literals, array, object, function, snippet, or unknown), its type as the source writes it, its default after =, and required when it has neither a default nor an optional type. A component whose props cannot be read, such as one that does not parse, is listed with the reason. A component with examples, named sets of its props in its examples file under design/components (ADR-0164), is listed with how many it has. A sub-project of any other kind is listed as unsupported, with its kind.

Props are read by a script flai embeds, run with node in the sub-project's folder on the sub-project's own svelte/compiler; no component is run. So node must be on PATH and svelte installed in each Svelte sub-project listed: when either is missing, list fails, exit status 1, saying what to install.

--json prints {"projects": [{"name", "path", "kind", "supported", "setup", "components": [{"project", "path", "name", "props": [{"name", "kind", "type", "default", "required", "literals", "skeleton"}], "error", "examples": [{"name", "props", "theme", "width", "answers"}], "examples\_path"}]}]}, setup only when the sub-project names one, and type, default, literals, error, theme, width, and answers only when they have a value. answers are the answers the component harness gives the component's requests to the app's own server (ADR-0187), as the file has them. skeleton is given for each array, object, and unknown prop only: an empty value of its type, which flai resolves with the sub-project's own typescript, or [], {}, or null where it cannot. examples\_path is the component's examples file, design/components/&lt;sub-project&gt;/&lt;its path, .svelte made .examples.json&gt;, whether or not it exists, and examples is [] when it does not. A file that does not fit the format gives the examples that parsed, props {} where they are not an object and answers left out where they are not an array, and flai check reports what does not fit; one that cannot be read fails list.

Examples:

```bash
flai components list
flai components list --project flaiover
flai components list --json
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--project` string | list only the sub-project of this name, one of the manifest's projects |

#### flai components serve

Run a Svelte sub-project's own Vite dev server with flai's component harness, in the foreground.

```text
flai components serve [flags]
```

Run the Vite dev server of the sub-project --project names with flai's component harness, in the foreground, until Ctrl-C or SIGTERM stops it. The sub-project is one of kind sveltekit or svelte in system-flow.yaml; --project may be left out when the manifest has one such sub-project only.

flai writes a Vite config under .flai-cache/components/&lt;project&gt;/&lt;sub-project&gt;/ that loads the sub-project's own Vite config and merges flai's harness plugin into it, then runs the sub-project's own vite, from its node\_modules, in its folder, on 127.0.0.1 and a free port (ADR-0163). Once the harness answers, it prints the harness's URL, the port's /\_\_flai/components/ on 127.0.0.1, and under it the sub-project and how to stop it. Open the URL with ?c=&lt;path&gt;, a component's path in the sub-project as flai components list prints it, to render that component after the components key's setup module; a saved change reaches the page as a hot update. Vite's own output goes to standard error.

--story serves the sub-project in that story's worktree instead, by the manifest its branch holds, on a port of its own, so that it runs beside the main checkout's (S-0442). The story must be in progress or in review and have a worktree; one without is refused with how to open it (flai stream open). A worktree is a fresh checkout, so when the sub-project's vite is not installed there flai first installs its dependencies by the lock file found in its folder or one above it, up to the worktree's root: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile for pnpm-lock.yaml, npm ci for package-lock.json, yarn install --frozen-lockfile for yarn.lock. A failed install is the command's error, with its last lines of output.

This runs the project's code and its dependencies on this machine, as the sub-project's own dev server does, reachable from this machine only. The dashboard has flai serve start the same dev server only once the operator turns the components host action on (flai serve enable components).

A sub-project without vite installed is refused with what to install, and a dev server that exits on its own ends the command, exit status 1, with its last lines of output. --json prints {"project", "url", "port", "pid"}, and "story" with --story, once the harness answers.

Examples:

```bash
flai components serve
flai components serve --project flaiover
flai components serve --project flaiover --json
flai components serve --project flaiover --story S-0042
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--project` string | serve the sub-project of this name, of kind sveltekit or svelte; needed when the manifest has more than one |
| `--story` string | serve it in this story's worktree, installing its dependencies there first when they are missing; the story must be in progress or in review |

### flai config

Read and write ~/.flai/config.json.

Read and write the flai configuration file: ~/.flai/config.json, or the path in --config or FLAI\_CONFIG. The first command that needs it creates it with defaults. Unknown keys are refused.

```text
Keys:
  template.repo
  template.ref
  dashboard.image
  dashboard.tag
  dashboard.port
  dashboard.bind
  dashboard.no_restart
  dashboard.allow_unsigned
  dashboard.push_key
  dashboard.push_known_hosts
  dashboard.allowed_hosts
  cache_dir
  author
  worktrees.relative_paths
```

dashboard.push\_key and dashboard.push\_known\_hosts are retired and ignored (ADR-0031); they stay settable so an old value can be cleared. The same file holds host\_actions, agent, checks, and import\_roots, which flai serve enable, disable, agent, checks, and import manage.

Subcommands:

- [get](#flai-config-get): Print the whole config, or one dotted key
- [path](#flai-config-path): Print the config file path in use
- [set](#flai-config-set): Set one dotted key and save

#### flai config get

Print the whole config, or one dotted key.

```text

```

Examples:

```bash

flai config get template.repo
flai config get dashboard --json
```

#### flai config path

Print the config file path in use.

```text

```

#### flai config set

Set one dotted key and save.

```text

```

Examples:

```bash

```

### flai criteria

List, tick, and untick an item's acceptance criteria by their numbers.

An item's acceptance criteria are the checkboxes under its ## Acceptance criteria heading, numbered from 1 in the order they appear, as flai criteria list prints them. An agent ticks a criterion once it has verified it, and not before (work-management.md); flai criteria tick changes that one box and every other byte of the body stays as it was.

tick and untick are an edit of the body, made as flai edit makes one: an archived or closed item is refused (exit 4), as is a finding the change introduces inside the story, as flai edit says; with --hash, a change someone made meanwhile is a conflict (exit 3); and agents connected over MCP are told the criteria changed. A number there is not is refused, and nothing is written.

The MCP tool criteria\_tick and the dashboard tick and untick criteria the same way.

Examples:

```bash
flai criteria list S-0282
flai criteria tick S-0282 1 3
flai criteria tick S-0282 1,3 --autocommit
flai criteria untick S-0282 2
flai criteria list S-0282 --json
```

Subcommands:

- [list](#flai-criteria-list): Print an item's acceptance criteria, numbered, and which are ticked
- [tick](#flai-criteria-tick): Tick an item's acceptance criteria by the numbers flai criteria list prints
- [untick](#flai-criteria-untick): Untick an item's acceptance criteria by the numbers flai criteria list prints

#### flai criteria list

Print an item's acceptance criteria, numbered, and which are ticked.

```text
flai criteria list <id>
```

#### flai criteria tick

Tick an item's acceptance criteria by the numbers flai criteria list prints.

```text
flai criteria tick <id> <n>... [flags]
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--autocommit` | commit the item, unless dashboard.autocommit is false |
| `--by` string | who ticks, as agents are told (default: FLAI\_AGENT, then the config author) |
| `--hash` string | the hash flai criteria list --json or flai edit --show printed; a change made meanwhile is then a conflict |
| `--trailer` stringArray | trailer line for the commit (repeatable) |

#### flai criteria untick

Untick an item's acceptance criteria by the numbers flai criteria list prints.

```text
flai criteria untick <id> <n>... [flags]
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--autocommit` | commit the item, unless dashboard.autocommit is false |
| `--by` string | who ticks, as agents are told (default: FLAI\_AGENT, then the config author) |
| `--hash` string | the hash flai criteria list --json or flai edit --show printed; a change made meanwhile is then a conflict |
| `--trailer` stringArray | trailer line for the commit (repeatable) |

### flai dashboard

Make sure the one flaiover dashboard runs and serves this project.

```text
flai dashboard [flags]
```

One dashboard container serves every project on this host (S-0080): if it is not running, this pulls the image (unless missing) and starts it, published on every interface (--bind 127.0.0.1 to restrict) on the configured port; if it already runs, for this project or another, this registers the project with it and starts no second container. The container is given that port, the one login token, and the one credential flai serve proves itself with, kept beside flai serve's state, and nothing else: no file of any project is mounted into it (ADR-0031). Everything it shows and changes it asks of flai serve on this host, which this command registers the project with; it starts flai host, which runs flai serve and the MCP servers, when none runs (S-0106). Image, tag, port, and bind come from flags, then the dashboard section of system-flow.yaml, then config; they matter only the first time, when they decide what the shared container is started with.

For ghcr.io/bytepunx/flaiover, the default image, the tag names a flaiover release: latest is the newest, X.Y.Z that one. flai downloads the release's digest list, verifies its signature with the key built into it, and pulls and runs ghcr.io/bytepunx/flaiover@sha256:&lt;digest&gt; (ADR-0070). Any other tag, or a release with no list this flai can verify, is refused, saying why, and nothing starts. When the releases cannot be reached, a list verified before and kept beside flai serve's state is used, and that is said. --build, and --image naming another repository, run image:tag as given and are reported unsigned.

The container serves a flai with no release stamp, a development build such as scripts/flai.sh builds, only when it is started with FLAIOVER\_ALLOW\_UNSIGNED=1: with dashboard.allow\_unsigned on, in the manifest's dashboard section or else in config, with --build, or with --allow-unsigned, for this start only, which writes nothing to the configuration. flai dashboard restart, flai dashboard upgrade, and flai host's restart keep it for the container they start again.

Examples:

```bash
flai dashboard
flai dashboard --tag 0.42.3      # that flaiover release, run by digest
flai dashboard --port 8080 --pull
flai dashboard --attach          # stream logs until Ctrl-C (the container keeps running)
flai dashboard --build           # build flaiover:local from this monorepo instead of pulling
flai dashboard --allow-unsigned  # serve a flai with no release stamp, for this start only
flai dashboard stop
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--allow-unsigned` | allow unsigned builds for this start only, without writing the configuration: the container serves a flai with no release stamp |
| `--attach` | follow the container logs after starting |
| `--bind` string | host address to publish on, 0.0.0.0 for every interface (default: manifest, then config, then 0.0.0.0) |
| `--build` | build the image from flaiover/ in this repository as flaiover:local and run that; unsigned builds are allowed for it |
| `--image` string | image repository; one other than ghcr.io/bytepunx/flaiover runs its tag as given, unsigned (default: manifest, then config) |
| `--no-serve` | do not register the project with flai serve or start flai host; the dashboard then has no flai on the host to ask (ADR-0029) |
| `--open` | open the dashboard in a browser |
| `--port` int | host port to publish (default: manifest, then config) |
| `--pull` | pull the image even if present |
| `--tag` string | latest or a flaiover release X.Y.Z, run by digest from its signed list; for another --image, its tag (default: manifest, then config) |

Subcommands:

- [check](#flai-dashboard-check): Report whether a newer dashboard image is available, without changing anything
- [logs](#flai-dashboard-logs): Print the dashboard container's logs
- [restart](#flai-dashboard-restart): Stop and start the dashboard container again, with whatever image it is already running
- [status](#flai-dashboard-status): Show whether the dashboard container runs and answers: running, not answering, or gone
- [stop](#flai-dashboard-stop): Stop this project's dashboard; the shared container stops only when it was the last project served
- [token](#flai-dashboard-token): Print the dashboard token and login link; --rotate replaces it
- [upgrade](#flai-dashboard-upgrade): Pull a newer dashboard image, or a chosen release, and swap to it, only once it answers healthy
- [versions](#flai-dashboard-versions): List the published dashboard releases, marking the running, the configured, and the not deployable ones

#### flai dashboard check

Report whether a newer dashboard image is available, without changing anything.

```text
flai dashboard check [flags]
```

Resolves the configured (or --tag) tag as flai dashboard does and compares the result with what the running container runs. For ghcr.io/bytepunx/flaiover it verifies the release's signed digest list and asks whether a digest of the running image is on it, pulling nothing; a release refused is an error saying why. For --image naming another repository it pulls the tag and compares image IDs, and reports the image unsigned. Changes nothing: flai dashboard upgrade applies it. Reports plainly, not as an error, when the container is not running.

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--image` string | image name (default: manifest, then config) |
| `--tag` string | latest or a flaiover release X.Y.Z to check against; for another --image, its tag (default: manifest, then config) |

#### flai dashboard logs

Print the dashboard container's logs.

```text
flai dashboard logs [flags]
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `-f`, `--follow` | follow the log output |

#### flai dashboard restart

Stop and start the dashboard container again, with whatever image it is already running.

```text
flai dashboard restart [flags]
```

Cycles the shared dashboard container's process without changing its image: if it is running, this stops it and starts again the exact image it was running, by its image ID, never a fresh pull and never what its tag names now, so a floating tag such as latest cannot silently upgrade it, even after flai dashboard check pulled a newer one; flai dashboard upgrade does that deliberately. It still names the reference the image was started for: for a flaiover release, ghcr.io/bytepunx/flaiover@sha256:&lt;digest&gt;. If it is not running, this starts the dashboard flai last recorded, by its image ID while that is still here, else by its reference, without resolving dashboard.tag again; with no record, or with --image or --tag, it starts what flai dashboard would, a release refused starting nothing. Every project registered with flai serve keeps its registration: only the container's process restarts. It allows unsigned builds (FLAIOVER\_ALLOW\_UNSIGNED=1) when the start it repeats did, by --allow-unsigned, --build, or the setting, or dashboard.allow\_unsigned is on now, and gives it dashboard.allowed\_hosts as the configuration has it now (FLAIOVER\_ALLOWED\_HOSTS), so a changed list applies.

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--bind` string | host address to publish on (default: manifest, then config, then 0.0.0.0) |
| `--image` string | image name (default: manifest, then config) |
| `--port` int | host port to publish (default: manifest, then config) |
| `--tag` string | latest or a flaiover release X.Y.Z, when no container runs; for another --image, its tag (default: manifest, then config) |

#### flai dashboard status

Show whether the dashboard container runs and answers: running, not answering, or gone.

```text
flai dashboard status
```

Asks docker whether the shared dashboard container runs, and its published port whether /\_health answers (S-0184): running when it does, not answering when the container runs and it does not, gone when no container runs. Docker's own verdict from the image's HEALTHCHECK is shown beside it. flai host restarts a dashboard that is gone or not answering unless dashboard.no\_restart is set. For a running container it shows its image's digest and the flaiover release whose signed digest list, kept beside flai serve's state, names it, or that it is unsigned. While flai serve runs, a line beside it says what flai serve did with that image at its last dial (S-0238): dials it, signed; refused it, as the dashboard runs an unsigned image no signed list names; or image not measured, as Docker where flai serve runs cannot say what the dashboard runs, with why, so the release stamp alone is checked. --json gives that verdict as serve\_image. Under dashboard.allow\_unsigned (S-0239) it says "unsigned allowed: started with FLAIOVER\_ALLOW\_UNSIGNED=1" for a container started so, and under the host flai's connection the sides it admitted without a release stamp: "unsigned allowed: flai", "dashboard", or "flai and dashboard"; a signed pair shows neither. --json gives the container's as allow\_unsigned and the connection's sides as host\_flai.unsigned. For a running container it says the hosts it accepts beside its own address, as it was started with them (FLAIOVER\_ALLOWED\_HOSTS), and when dashboard.allowed\_hosts names others now, which flai dashboard restart applies (S-0489); --json gives the container's list as allowed\_hosts, "" for none.

#### flai dashboard stop

Stop this project's dashboard; the shared container stops only when it was the last project served.

```text
flai dashboard stop
```

#### flai dashboard token

Print the dashboard token and login link; --rotate replaces it.

```text
flai dashboard token [flags]
```

One token for every project the dashboard serves (S-0080), created by flai dashboard on first run and kept beside flai serve's state, next to flai's config file. Browsers use the login link, whose fragment never leaves the browser; agents send it as a bearer header. --rotate writes a new token in place and restarts the dashboard, which ends every session, for every project it serves, not only this one. With --no-restart the dashboard is not restarted, and keeps the old token until it is told the new one: its settings page rotates it that way and keeps its own session.

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--no-restart` | with --rotate, leave the dashboard running: it is told the new token another way (S-0105, from its settings page) |
| `--rotate` | replace the token and restart the dashboard, for every project it serves |

#### flai dashboard upgrade

Pull a newer dashboard image, or a chosen release, and swap to it, only once it answers healthy.

```text
flai dashboard upgrade [flags]
```

Resolves the configured (or --tag) tag as flai dashboard does. For ghcr.io/bytepunx/flaiover that is latest, the newest flaiover release, or a release X.Y.Z, whose signed digest list flai verifies; a release refused is refused before anything is pulled, saying why. When no digest of the running image is on the list, it pulls the release's image by digest, ghcr.io/bytepunx/flaiover@sha256:&lt;digest&gt;. For --image naming another repository it pulls the tag and compares image IDs, and reports the image unsigned. When the image differs from what is running, it starts it as a second, temporary container on a loopback port of its own, waits for it to answer /\_health, and only then stops the running container and starts the new image at the real name and port. The running container is never stopped until the replacement has proven healthy: if it does not become healthy in time, the temporary container is removed and the running one is left exactly as it was, and this reports why. Should the new image then fail to start at the real name, the previous image is started there again, and this still fails, saying so. The new container allows unsigned builds (FLAIOVER\_ALLOW\_UNSIGNED=1) when the one it replaces was started allowing them, or dashboard.allow\_unsigned is on now, and is given dashboard.allowed\_hosts as the configuration has it now (FLAIOVER\_ALLOWED\_HOSTS).

--tag deploys that release, an earlier one included, the same way, for this container once: dashboard.tag is not changed, so an upgrade without a tag uses the configured one again (pin with flai config set dashboard.tag). With --published the tag must be a published dashboard release, the bare X.Y.Z of a flaiover/vX.Y.Z tag (flai dashboard versions lists them): any other is refused, naming the published ones, and so is one with no digest list this flai can verify, naming why and the deployable ones, before anything is pulled. Only an --image of another repository, such as a mirror's, runs a tag as given, unsigned.

Examples:

```bash
flai dashboard upgrade
flai dashboard upgrade --published --tag 0.4.0
flai dashboard upgrade --image registry.example.com/flaiover --tag my-mirror-build
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--bind` string | host address to publish on (default: manifest, then config, then 0.0.0.0) |
| `--image` string | image name (default: manifest, then config) |
| `--port` int | host port to publish (default: manifest, then config) |
| `--published` | refuse a --tag that is not a published dashboard release, before anything is pulled |
| `--repo` string | GitHub repository whose flaiover/vX.Y.Z tags are the published dashboard releases (with --published) (default `bytepunx/system-flow`) |
| `--tag` string | latest or a flaiover release X.Y.Z to upgrade to, for this container once; for another --image, its tag (default: manifest, then config) |

#### flai dashboard versions

List the published dashboard releases, marking the running, the configured, and the not deployable ones.

```text
flai dashboard versions [flags]
```

Lists the published dashboard releases, the repository's flaiover/vX.Y.Z tags, newest first, and installs nothing. Each release's image tag is its bare version, X.Y.Z. It marks the newest, the release the running container's image carries (its FLAIOVER\_VERSION, else its image tag), and the configured tag (flags, then the dashboard section of system-flow.yaml, then config). It marks "not deployable", with the reason, each release with no digest list this flai can verify, such as one from before signing (ADR-0070): flai dashboard refuses to run it. To check, it downloads each release's digest list and its signature; a download that fails fails the list. Docker is not needed to list: without it, or with no container running, nothing is marked running. flai dashboard upgrade --published --tag X.Y.Z deploys one of them, an earlier one included, for that container once; dashboard.tag is not changed. With --json it prints a list of version, tag, running, configured, and latest, and, for a release that is not deployable, unverifiable, signature (missing, bad, or unknown-key), and reason.

Examples:

```bash
flai dashboard versions
flai dashboard versions --json
flai dashboard upgrade --published --tag 0.4.0
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--repo` string | GitHub repository whose flaiover/vX.Y.Z tags are the published dashboard releases (default `bytepunx/system-flow`) |

### flai design

Write, show, and render the project's design system.

A project's design system is its tokens, the values its UI uses, and its guidance, the words that say when to use which (ADR-0146). The tokens are one DTCG 2025.10 file the manifest's design.tokens names, design/system/design-system.tokens.json when it is unset; the guidance is design/system/design-system.md. flai check validates the token file as design.tokens; flai design init writes both from starters, flai design show reports them with each colour role pair's contrast, and flai design css renders the tokens as CSS. flai design css --write writes the tokens to the generated design stylesheet the manifest's design.stylesheet names, which flai check reports as design.stale when it falls behind the tokens (ADR-0159). flai design init and flai file save, whenever they write the token file, write the stylesheet from it too (ADR-0150).

A story proposes a change to the design system on its branch: flai design proposals lists the open stories whose branches change it, and flai design show --story S-nnnn reads the design system a story proposes from its worktree. Accepting the story merges its branch, and with it the proposal.

Examples:

```bash
flai design init --topics flaiover
flai design show
flai design show --json
flai design show --story S-0042
flai design proposals
flai design css --tailwind
flai design css --write
```

Subcommands:

- [css](#flai-design-css): Print the tokens as CSS custom properties or a Tailwind v4 @theme block, or write the design stylesheet
- [init](#flai-design-init): Write the token file and the guidance from flai's starters, and the design stylesheet when one is named
- [proposals](#flai-design-proposals): List the open stories whose branches change the design system
- [show](#flai-design-show): Report the token file, the guidance, the problems, and each role pair's contrast

#### flai design css

Print the tokens as CSS custom properties or a Tailwind v4 @theme block, or write the design stylesheet.

```text
flai design css [flags]
```

Print the token file's tokens as CSS custom properties with Tailwind v4's names, such as --color-primary and --text-sm, one block per theme, each with every token: :root for light, then [data-theme='dark'] for dark. With --tailwind, print them as a Tailwind v4 stylesheet: a @custom-variant rule that makes Tailwind's dark: variant follow [data-theme='dark'], a @theme block of the light values, then a [data-theme='dark'] block of the dark values that differ from them, so that the dark values and the dark: variant follow the same attribute (ADR-0159).

With --write, write the design stylesheet instead of printing: the file the manifest's design.stylesheet names, holding what --tailwind prints with a header ahead of it that says the file is generated from the token file by flai design css --write and is not to be edited. It creates the file's folders and replaces what is there, since the file is generated, and prints the path written; with --json, {"stylesheet": ..., "tokens": ...}. When the manifest names no stylesheet, --write writes nothing and exits with status 1: set design.stylesheet in system-flow.yaml to the stylesheet's repository path, such as web/src/theme.css. Once the stylesheet is there, flai check reports design.stale whenever it falls behind the tokens; run flai design css --write again to bring it up to date. --write and --tailwind are mutually exclusive.

No token file is an error, exit status 1, naming the file and flai design init. So is a token file with problems: css renders and writes nothing rather than CSS that silently leaves out or misreads a token, and the error lists each problem, as flai design show and flai check report them; fix them and run it again.

Examples:

```bash
flai design css
flai design css --tailwind
flai design css --write
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--tailwind` | print a Tailwind v4 stylesheet, the dark: variant, a @theme block, and the dark values, instead of one block of custom properties per theme; --write writes it |
| `--write` | write the Tailwind v4 stylesheet, with a generated-file header, to the file the manifest's design.stylesheet names |

#### flai design init

Write the token file and the guidance from flai's starters, and the design stylesheet when one is named.

```text
flai design init [flags]
```

Write the token file the manifest's design.tokens names, and the guidance, design/system/design-system.md, from flai's starters, creating their folders.

The token file is a DTCG 2025.10 resolver document: one set of light values and the theme modifier, whose dark context overrides each colour role and each shadow. It holds every required token: the colour roles, the sans and mono font stacks (system stacks, no web fonts), the type scale xs to 4xl, the spacing step, and the radii and shadows sm, md, and lg, at Tailwind v4's default sizes. Every role pair passes its contrast threshold in light and dark. The guidance has the headings a design system's words go under, each saying what to write there, and its front matter's updated is today.

--topics sets the guidance's topics, all by default. The topics choose the stories flai prime gives the guidance to, so name the UI sub-project, or its kind, so that every story that touches the UI is given it.

--project names a sub-project the design system governs, one of the manifest's projects; repeat it or separate names with commas. init writes each name into the guidance's topics, the one list prime reads, so there is no second record of the sub-projects governed (ADR-0152). With --project and no --topics, the topics are the sub-projects alone, without all; with both, they are the --topics values, then each sub-project not among them. A name the manifest does not list is refused before anything is written.

When the manifest's design.stylesheet names a design stylesheet, init then writes it from the token file it has just written, as flai design css --write does, replacing what is there. When that fails, the token file and the guidance stay, and the error says to run flai design css --write.

When the token file or the guidance is there already, init writes nothing and says which, with exit status 1. It commits nothing. Prints the paths written, the token file, the guidance, and the stylesheet when there is one; with --json, {"tokens": ..., "guidance": ..., "topics": [...], "stylesheet": ...}, stylesheet left out when the manifest names none.

Examples:

```bash
flai design init
flai design init --topics flaiover,ui
flai design init --project flaiover
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--project` strings | a sub-project of the manifest the design system governs, written into the guidance's topics; repeatable |
| `--topics` strings | the guidance's topics, which choose the stories prime gives it to: name the UI sub-project (default `[all]`) |

#### flai design proposals

List the open stories whose branches change the design system.

```text
flai design proposals
```

List the proposals: the open stories whose branch, or whose worktree uncommitted, changes the design system, that is the token file, the guidance, or both, at the paths the main checkout's manifest gives. A story's branch is compared with its merge base with the main branch, as flai stream diff compares it, and git is read in the main checkout, so the list is the same from the main checkout and from any worktree. A story that is done or cancelled proposes nothing and is left out; so is every story of a project that is not a git repository, which has no branches.

The Design page lists the same through the host method design.proposals, and flai design show --story S-nnnn reads the design system a proposal holds from its story's worktree. A proposal needs no step of its own to land: accepting the story merges its branch, and with it the main checkout's design system becomes the proposal's.

Prints a table of ID, STATE, TITLE, and CHANGES, the paths the story changes, in story ID order, or a line saying no open story's branch changes the design system, naming the token file and the guidance. With --json, the list as the host method design.proposals answers it: [{id, title, status, paths}], [] when there are none.

Examples:

```bash
flai design proposals
flai design proposals --json
```

#### flai design show

Report the token file, the guidance, the problems, and each role pair's contrast.

```text
flai design show [flags]
```

Report the project's design system: the token file's path, the guidance's path and its headings, the number of tokens in each theme, each problem flai check reports as design.tokens, as &lt;file&gt;:&lt;line&gt;: &lt;token path&gt;: &lt;message&gt;, and, for light and dark, each colour role pair's contrast ratio against ADR-0148's threshold: 4.5:1 for text, muted text, each state on background, surface, and its tint, and on-primary and on-secondary on their fill; 3:1 for border and focus on background. A pair whose oklch colour lies outside sRGB is computed on the colour clipped to sRGB, and says so.

Contrast is a report, never a finding: a pair below its threshold is FAIL in the table and the exit status is still 0. So is a token file with problems, which flai check reports as findings; show prints them and exits 0. No token file is no error either: show says so and how to write one.

With --story S-nnnn, show reads the design system a story proposes from the story's worktree instead of the main checkout, at the token file and guidance paths the worktree's manifest gives, and names the story and its worktree first; the host method design.get does the same when given a story. It works the same from the main checkout and from any worktree. It refuses, with exit status 1, an ID that is no story of this project, a story that is done or cancelled, which proposes nothing, and a story with no worktree, which flai stream open S-nnnn opens. flai design proposals lists the stories whose branches change the design system.

--json prints what the host method design.get answers: {path, exists, no\_token\_file, guidance, stylesheet, headings, resolver, themes: [{name, tokens: [{path, type, value, css, variables, ref, line}]}], problems, css, tailwind, contrast: [{theme, pairs: [{theme, foreground, background, foreground\_hex, background\_hex, ratio, threshold, passes, clipped}]}]}, the same with --story. stylesheet is the manifest's design.stylesheet, left out when it names none.

Examples:

```bash
flai design show
flai design show --json
flai design show --story S-0042
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--story` string | read the design system the open story S-nnnn proposes, from its worktree, instead of the main checkout's |

### flai digest

Record and read the digest: the facts past stories learned (ADR-0191).

The digest is one markdown file per fact a story learned, D-nnnn-&lt;slug&gt;.md in the design folder's digest folder (ADR-0191): a decision, the operator's answer on a thread, a recommendation the operator confirmed or overruled, or an issue's cause and fix. flai writes and checks each entry's front matter, and nothing in the folder is ever deleted.

Subcommands:

- [edit](#flai-digest-edit): Change a digest entry's body, topics, paths, sources, or asked\_again
- [harvest](#flai-digest-harvest): List the facts the digest could record: answers, recommendations, decisions, and causes
- [list](#flai-digest-list): List the digest's entries with their sources, topics, paths, date, and status
- [new](#flai-digest-new): Record a digest entry: its ID, file, and front matter are supplied
- [seed](#flai-digest-seed): Write a digest entry for each operator answer and closed issue's cause no entry records yet
- [show](#flai-digest-show): Print a digest entry: its front matter and its body

#### flai digest edit

Change a digest entry's body, topics, paths, sources, or asked\_again.

```text
flai digest edit <D-nnnn> [flags]
```

Change a digest entry in the checkout it runs in. Each flag given replaces that part of the entry, and leaves the rest of the file as it was: --body or --body-file the text below the heading, and --topic, --path, --source, and --asked-again their lists, each repeatable or comma separated. Give a list flag an empty value, such as --topic=, to empty it. The ID may be written in any padding: D-7 is D-0007.

The check runs on what was written: when it reports a problem the change introduced, the file is put back as it was, each problem is printed, and the exit code is 4.

Examples:

```bash
flai digest edit D-0007 --topic cli --topic go
flai digest edit D-0007 --asked-again TH-0512 --asked-again TH-0530 --json
flai digest edit D-0007 --body-file - < body.md
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--asked-again` strings | thread that asked what the entry already answered; replaces the entry's asked\_again (repeatable, or comma separated) |
| `--body` string | the text below the heading: what was asked or decided, the answer and its reason, and links to its sources |
| `--body-file` string | read the text below the heading from this file, or from standard input when it is - |
| `--path` strings | repository path the fact bears on; replaces the entry's paths (repeatable, or comma separated) |
| `--source` strings | work item, thread, or issue the fact comes from; replaces the entry's sources (repeatable, or comma separated) |
| `--topic` strings | topic the fact bears on; replaces the entry's topics (repeatable, or comma separated) |

#### flai digest harvest

List the facts the digest could record: answers, recommendations, decisions, and causes.

```text
flai digest harvest [flags]
```

List every candidate for the digest in this checkout, learned on or after --since, or every one when it is not given: the operator's answers and the recommendations the operator overruled on every thread, resolved or not, the decisions in done stories' narratives, and the causes and fixes of closed issues. It is deterministic and writes nothing, so the curator reads the same list every run.

Each line gives the candidate's kind, its date, its source with where in it (the thread entry's time, or the narrative's path), its title, and the entries that already cite the source; the last line counts them by kind. --since is a day, YYYY-MM-DD in UTC, or an RFC 3339 time. --kind keeps the candidates of that kind (decision, answer, recommendation, cause), repeatable or comma separated. --json gives an array of the candidates with every field, their topics, paths, and text included, [] when none.

Examples:

```bash
flai digest harvest --since 2026-10-01
flai digest harvest --kind answer,recommendation --json
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--kind` strings | only the candidates of this kind: decision, answer, recommendation, cause (repeatable, or comma separated) |
| `--since` string | only the candidates learned on or after this day, YYYY-MM-DD in UTC, or this RFC 3339 time |

#### flai digest list

List the digest's entries with their sources, topics, paths, date, and status.

```text
flai digest list [flags]
```

List the entries in this checkout's digest folder, in ID order: each one's ID, status, kind, date, and title, and below it its sources, topics, and paths. --status keeps the entries in that status (active, absorbed, compacted); --topic keeps those that bear on the topic. --json gives an array of the entries, bodies included, [] when none.

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--status` string | only the entries in this status: active, absorbed, compacted |
| `--topic` string | only the entries that bear on this topic |

#### flai digest new

Record a digest entry: its ID, file, and front matter are supplied.

```text
flai digest new "<fact>" --kind <kind> --source <id>... [flags]
```

Record one fact a story learned as a new digest entry, in the checkout it runs in. The ID is one more than the highest D-nnnn in this checkout, on main, in any worktree, and on any story branch, so parallel writers do not take the same one; gaps are not filled. The file is D-nnnn-&lt;slug&gt;.md in the digest folder, dated today, with status active.

--kind is what the fact is: decision, answer, recommendation, cause. --source names the work items (E-, S-, T-), threads (TH-), and issues (I-) it comes from, at least one, each in the project or its archive. --source, --topic, and --path are repeatable, or comma separated. The body is a few sentences below the heading; it says where a secret lives, never its value.

The check runs on what was written: when it reports anything, such as a source that names nothing or text with the shape of a key or token, the file is removed, each problem is printed, and the exit code is 4.

Examples:

```bash
flai digest new "Story worktrees install with the project's pnpm store" --kind cause --source I-0177 --source S-0481 --topic flaiover --path scripts/flaiover-install.sh
flai digest new "The digest lives under design/digest" --kind answer --source TH-0476 --body-file answer.md --json
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--body` string | the text below the heading: what was asked or decided, the answer and its reason, and links to its sources |
| `--body-file` string | read the text below the heading from this file, or from standard input when it is - |
| `--kind` string | what the fact is: decision, answer, recommendation, cause |
| `--path` strings | repository path the fact bears on, from the project root (repeatable, or comma separated) |
| `--source` strings | work item (E-, S-, T-), thread (TH-), or issue (I-) the fact comes from (repeatable, or comma separated; at least one) |
| `--topic` strings | topic the fact bears on, as a story's are (repeatable, or comma separated) |

#### flai digest seed

Write a digest entry for each operator answer and closed issue's cause no entry records yet.

```text
flai digest seed [flags]
```

Seed the digest in the checkout it runs in from what harvest lists, learned on or after --since, or all of it when it is not given. It writes an answer or recommendation entry for each answer the operator gave on a thread, and a cause entry for each closed issue with a cause and a fix, each dated the day it was learned and quoting its source. It never seeds decisions: a model judges which of them a design document already records.

A source an entry already records is skipped: an issue any entry cites, or a thread's answer when an entry citing the thread holds the answer's time. So a second run writes nothing. Each entry is checked as flai digest new checks it; one the check refuses, such as an answer with the shape of a key or token, is skipped and named by the rules it broke, never its text, and the rest are written.

Each entry written is printed with its ID, kind, source, and title, and each skipped one with its reason, then the candidates listed, written, and skipped by kind. --dry-run prints what would be written and writes nothing. --json gives the result: listed by kind, written, skipped, and dry\_run. A skipped entry is not an error: the exit code is 0 unless the seed fails.

Examples:

```bash
flai digest seed --dry-run
flai digest seed --since 2026-10-01 --json
```

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--dry-run` | print what would be written and write nothing |
| `--since` string | only the candidates learned on or after this day, YYYY-MM-DD in UTC, or this RFC 3339 time |

#### flai digest show

Print a digest entry: its front matter and its body.

```text
flai digest show <D-nnnn>
```
